sentences.show: They fed him enough poison to kill five men. They shot him. They threw him into an icy river. At least, that's the legend.
His name was Grigori Rasputin, a peasant from Siberia with wild eyes, who said he could heal with prayer.
The Tsar's only son, Alexei, had haemophilia. The smallest cut could kill him.
In 1912, the boy was dying. Rasputin sent a telegram, and Alexei recovered. No one knows why.
From then on, the Empress believed he was sent by God. Half of Russia believed he was the devil.
In December 1916, a group of nobles led by Prince Felix Yusupov decided to kill him.
Yusupov's story: he gave Rasputin cakes and wine laced with cyanide. Nothing happened.
So he shot him in the chest. Later, the "body" leapt up and attacked him.
Rasputin ran into the snow. They shot him again, and threw him off a bridge into the frozen river.
Days later, police found his body under the ice.
But the autopsy tells a different story. No poison. No water in his lungs.
He died from a bullet to the forehead, fired at close range. Before he ever hit the water.
His daughter said he never even ate sweets.
Fourteen months later, the Romanovs were gone. So was the Russian Empire.
So was Rasputin unkillable? Or did his killer just tell a better story?
Rasputin wouldn't stay down. Neither will we. Subscribe.
